doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Joining Thad Jones and the Liberian knighthood
summary: Joined the Thad Jones band through Hank Jones, then toured Liberia with Jimmy Randolph and was given knighthood by the President.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: In 1970 — well tell me about your knighthood.

Oh that was a great experience for me. In 1969 I had been with the Thad Jones band for about two and a half, not quite three years, because Hank [Jones] started with him even though Thad and I talked about my being part of the band before he hired Hank, when he finally did it he hired Hank. But Hank was busy with television and couldn’t do it all the time so every time he couldn’t do it he’d call me and say, “Roland, would you take over for me?” Of course I took over. And finally sometime in ’66 I had a lot of students, I told Hank I’m busy, I’ve got students, and if you can’t do this gig let me know so I can arrange to do it every Monday. So Hank said okay, you’ve got it. And I started working with the band. And this association with the band, it sort of branched out. A lot of people

began to hear me play and one night in my studio on 73rd Street in Manhattan, somebody called and asked me if I would consider coming to Liberia to play concerts. And of course I said yes immediately. There was no money involved. They had no money to pay. But they needed some people to play. And it turned out that they were asking people from various countries to contribute their part in the concert situation so they could raise money to build schools in Monrovia. And Jimmy Randolph or James Cheatham, I don’t know if you know that name but he was an actor in “Guys and Dolls” on Broadway, he’s a singer. And we went together. We met several people from Turkey, people from Germany, people from France, acrobats from Italy who did live wire. So it was not a circus but they put on a show and we were part of the show. We would perform songs from Randolph’s “Guys and Dolls” and then we’d sing pop tunes or whatever, and we went there for one week and the thing was so successful they kept us for another week. So we stayed in Liberia and moved from Liberia to Senegal to Cote d’Ivoire, we went to Guinea Bissau, we went to several countries close by. Liberia is only about 85 miles deep, about the size of New Jersey. And we went to several countries around and did performances. And they apparently raised quite a bit of money. Every other night they would have a big party at the Secretary of State’s house, Grimes was his name. His wife would put on a big spread, food I had never seen or tasted before. And so when the second week was over we were invited to the President’s house in Monrovia. He had a huge castle. And he had those 24-foot ceilings, you know, marble all over the flooring. It was just gorgeous. And he had myself and Jimmy Cheatham to come there and he asked us, he said, since we can’t give you money would you accept knighthood? And of course I said yes. So that’s how that happened. And when I came back home we got a telegram for me to come down to Washington, D.C. to the consulate, the Liberian consulate, and bring my family. And I went down and kneeled and they dubbed me knight commander you know, that’s what it is, and that experience, that gave me a great, big, huge emblem that was around my neck and somehow that disappeared. I didn’t lose it, I think somebody just took it. It had a big emblem on it and colors, the colors of the Liberian flag. And I don’t know where that is now. But the plaque, I have that. My wife hangs that on the wall. But I’m very proud of that because it means so much more than money. The money would have been spent that week. But this has lasted for thirty years, thirty one years. So that’s how that happened.
Did the citizens of those countries respond to what you played?
